title: Training Sentence Connections
description: Build parallel structures and connect clauses according to their logical relationship.
subject: rla
passage:
A department is preparing a short orientation for new employees. The draft agenda includes three goals: introducing the safety process, explaining how to request equipment, and showing employees where to report problems. Because the agenda will be read aloud and posted online, the editor wants its sentence patterns to be easy to follow.

Parallel structure helps readers recognize items that have the same role. If a sentence begins “The session will explain how to sign in, how to request a key, and how to report a hazard,” each item follows the same pattern. Mixing “to sign in,” “requesting a key,” and “how hazards are reported” makes the list harder to process even if the general meaning remains understandable.

The editor also checks how complete ideas are connected. Two independent clauses may be joined with a coordinating conjunction or separated with appropriate punctuation. A dependent idea should be attached to a complete clause rather than left as a fragment. The goal is not to make every sentence the same length. It is to show the relationship among ideas through balanced structure and deliberate connections.

questions.prompt: Choose the parallel revision: “The session covers signing in, how to request keys, and reporting hazards.”
questions.explanation: All three items use matching -ing forms: signing, requesting, and reporting.
questions.rule: Items in the same list should use the same grammatical pattern.

options.text: The session covers signing in, requesting keys, and reporting hazards.
The session covers to sign in, requesting keys, and hazards are reported.
options.whyWrong: The three items use different grammatical forms.

options.text: The session covers signing in, how to request keys, and hazards.
options.whyWrong: A gerund, a clause, and a noun do not form a parallel series.

options.text: The session covers sign in, requests for keys, and reporting hazards.
options.whyWrong: The items still do not use matching forms.

questions.prompt: The room was full, {{blank}} the trainer opened the second training area.
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the straightforward result relationship: the room was full, so another area was opened.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first—cause/result, contrast, addition—then choose the connector.

options.text: because
options.whyWrong: 'Because' would make the first fact a result of the second rather than showing the second action as a response.

options.text: although
options.whyWrong: 'Although' signals contrast, but the ideas show cause and result.

options.text: for example
options.whyWrong: 'For example' does not express the result relationship between the clauses.

options.text: so

questions.prompt: Complete the correlative structure: “The trainer will not only review the rules but also {{blank}}.”
questions.explanation: 'Review' and 'demonstrate' are parallel base verbs after 'will'.
questions.rule: With not only/but also, compare the grammatical form on both sides.

options.text: demonstrating the equipment
options.whyWrong: 'Review' is a base verb, so the paired element should also use a base verb.

options.text: a demonstration of the equipment
options.whyWrong: A noun phrase is not parallel with the verb 'review'.

options.text: demonstrate the equipment
the equipment will be demonstrated
options.whyWrong: The passive clause is not parallel with 'review the rules'.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly subordinates the reason?
questions.explanation: The dependent reason clause is attached to the independent clause with a comma, preserving the cause relationship.
questions.rule: A dependent clause beginning with because must attach to a complete clause.

options.text: Because the projector failed. The trainer used printed diagrams.
options.whyWrong: The dependent 'because' clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.

options.text: Because the projector failed, the trainer used printed diagrams.
The projector failed, because. The trainer used printed diagrams.
options.whyWrong: 'Because' cannot be left without the clause it introduces.

options.text: Because the projector failed; the trainer used printed diagrams.
options.whyWrong: A semicolon cannot join a dependent clause to an independent clause this way.

questions.explanation: All three actions use parallel base verbs after the shared modal 'should'.
questions.rule: Keep a shared helper verb such as should with the same form in every item.

options.text: Employees should arrive on time, bring identification, and to wear closed shoes.
options.whyWrong: The third item changes from a base verb to an infinitive.

options.text: Employees should arriving on time, bring identification, and closed shoes.
options.whyWrong: The three items use unrelated grammatical forms.

options.text: Employees should arrive on time, bring identification, and wear closed shoes.
Employees should arrive on time, identification is brought, and wear closed shoes.
options.whyWrong: The middle item changes into a clause rather than staying parallel with the verbs.

questions.prompt: Which revision best connects a contrast? “The training is brief. It covers the highest-risk tasks.”
questions.explanation: 'Although' preserves the intended contrast between the session's short duration and the importance of what it covers.
questions.rule: Choose the connector that states the relationship the ideas actually have.

options.text: Although the training is brief, it covers the highest-risk tasks.
Because the training is brief, it covers the highest-risk tasks.
options.whyWrong: This incorrectly turns the short duration into the cause of the coverage.

options.text: The training is brief, so it covers the highest-risk tasks.
options.whyWrong: 'So' signals cause/result rather than the intended contrast.

options.text: The training is brief; for example, it covers the highest-risk tasks.
options.whyWrong: The second idea is not an example of the first; it contrasts with it.

questions.prompt: Choose the revision that keeps the contrast and makes the actions parallel: “Although the checklist is shorter, it asks workers to inspect seals, recording pressure, and to report leaks, so rounds may be faster.”
questions.explanation: The revision keeps 'although' to preserve the contrast and uses the parallel verbs 'inspect, record, and report'; 'so' then preserves the cause/result relationship leading to the supervisor's expectation.
questions.rule: Hard edits can have two jobs at once: keep the form parallel and keep the logical relationships unchanged.

options.text: Because the checklist is shorter, it asks workers to inspect seals, record pressure, and report leaks, so rounds may be faster.
options.whyWrong: The actions are parallel, but 'because' changes the intended contrast into a cause relationship.

options.text: Although the checklist is shorter, it asks workers to inspect seals, recording pressure, and report leaks, so rounds may be faster.
options.whyWrong: 'Although' preserves the contrast, but 'recording' breaks the parallel verb series.

options.text: Although the checklist is shorter, it asks workers to inspect seals, record pressure, and report leaks, so rounds may be faster.
Although the checklist is shorter, workers inspect seals, pressure is recorded, and report leaks; however, rounds may be faster.
options.whyWrong: The connector adds an unnecessary second contrast, and the action series is not parallel.

questions.prompt: Choose the best revision: “The morning briefing was delayed; however, the trainer still managed to review lockout steps, demonstrating the alarm system, and to answer questions because the backup room was available.”
questions.explanation: 'However' preserves the contrast between the delay and the successful briefing, the verbs 'review, demonstrate, and answer' are parallel after 'managed to,' and 'because' correctly keeps the backup room as the reason the trainer could continue.
questions.rule: Check the whole sentence: parallel form, connector meaning, and cause/contrast must all survive the revision.

options.text: The morning briefing was delayed because the trainer still managed to review lockout steps, demonstrate the alarm system, and answer questions; however, the backup room was available.
options.whyWrong: The series is parallel, but 'because' incorrectly says the successful review caused the delay and moves the contrast away from the intended ideas.

options.text: The morning briefing was delayed; however, the trainer still managed to review lockout steps, demonstrate the alarm system, and answer questions because the backup room was available.
The morning briefing was delayed; however, the trainer still managed reviewing lockout steps, demonstrating the alarm system, and answering questions, although the backup room was available.
options.whyWrong: The forms after 'managed' are unidiomatic, and 'although' changes the backup room from a reason into a contrast.

options.text: Although the morning briefing was delayed, the trainer still managed to review lockout steps, demonstrating the alarm system, and answer questions, so the backup room was available.
options.whyWrong: The list is not parallel and 'so' reverses the cause relationship by making the room availability a result.
